doc.title: Milt Fillius interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 18, 2000

title: Swing era in 1935: paper routes, drums and buying records
summary: At 13 Fillius earned his own way, took up drums, formed a dance band and spent his money on Goodman, Shaw and Dorsey records.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Can you tell me when that first grabbed your attention? That music?

Well I was 13. And when I was 12 years of age my father said son, you are now going to earn your own way. You’re going to earn your keep and I’ll provide a roof over your head and food but you’ll earn your clothing, your spending money and so on, which he deemed to be a way to build character. So I started out and I had paper routes and an old thing called “Radio Mirror” magazine routes and I worked in a drug store and a grocery store. And I had a very busy time. Then I found the drums. And I started playing the drums and I took lessons from the guy who was the head percussionist with the Rochester Philharmonic, and my friend down the street and I formed a dance band. And so we went

out and for the rest of my time in high school we played a lot, made a lot — for those days — made a lot of money. You know you get five or ten bucks for a night and you thought oh geez I’m on top of the world. But I used all that money to buy records. And I just — there’s a record store in Rochester — Lovett’s I think is the name of it — and I drove them crazy. I spent every Saturday in the booths in there playing stuff and buying stuff. And I fell in love with Benny Goodman and Artie Shaw, the Dorseys, the whole bit. And I had a collection of records that was pretty damn good, which I retained until the war. And then when I went off to war my father got them and fortunately he taped all the 78s for me, and then we threw them away. But that’s how I got started.
